Como é escrita uma notícia: How a news story is written
PASSO 1: uma notícia tem partes fixas: o: STEP 1: a news story has fixed parts: the «titular» (headline), the subtitle, the «entradilla» (the lead, the first paragraph that sums everything up) and the «cuerpo» (the body). STEP 2: the lead answers five questions: ¿qué ocurrió?, ¿quién?, ¿dónde?, ¿cuándo? and ¿por qué? — the same "five Ws" as in English journalism. If you can answer all five, you've got the gist. STEP 3: headlines have their own style. Like English headlines, they use the present for past events and drop articles and auxiliaries: «Un incendio destruye una nave industrial» (Fire destroys warehouse) — more common in headlines than «Un incendio ha destruido…». STEP 4: in the body, the main event usually comes in the preterite (lesson 19): «El fuego comenzó a las ocho.» For something very recent, linked to the present, the present perfect appears: «Los bomberos han controlado el incendio.» STEP 5: with markers of finished past time (ayer, el lunes, la semana pasada) use the preterite: «Ayer inauguraron la biblioteca.» STEP 6: the passive and «se» (lesson 49) are frequent: «La biblioteca fue inaugurada ayer.», «Se investigan las causas.» (The causes are being investigated.) STEP 7: words: «periódico» and «diario» are the newspaper («diario» is also a personal diary); «papel» is paper as a material, never the newspaper. «Telediario» is the TV news in Spain. And "a piece of news" is simply «una noticia»; "the news" (in general) is «las noticias».
em português a manchete costuma usar o p: English "the news" is uncountable; in Spanish «noticia» is countable: «una noticia» (a piece of news), «las noticias» (the news). "The paper" is «el periódico», not «el papel». "According to the police" is «según la policía», with no preposition. And "fake news" is «bulo» (Spain) or «noticia falsa» (common in Latin America too).

Citar fontes e relatar o que se disse: Citing sources and reporting what was said
PASSO 1: para dizer de onde vem a inform: STEP 1: to say where information comes from, use «según» with no preposition after it: «Según la policía, no hay heridos.» (According to the police, no one was hurt.), «Según fuentes municipales, el proyecto costó dos millones.» STEP 2: the most common reporting verbs are «afirmar», «asegurar», «anunciar», «explicar», «declarar» and «añadir». They all take «que» and a verb in the indicative: «La alcaldesa anunció que abriría la biblioteca en octubre.» STEP 3: the sequence of tenses from lesson 48 still applies, much as in English reported speech: present becomes imperfect, preterite becomes pluperfect, future becomes conditional: «Dijo: Llegaremos pronto → Dijo que llegarían pronto.» STEP 4: when someone denies something, the next verb goes into the subjunctive, because you're not asserting the fact: «El club negó que el entrenador se fuera.» (The club denied that the coach was leaving.) English keeps the indicative here; Spanish doesn't. STEP 5: for unconfirmed information: «Dicen que…», «Se dice que…» (It's said that…), «Al parecer…» (Apparently…), «Parece ser que…». STEP 6: the press uses a "rumour conditional": «El accidente habría ocurrido de madrugada.» It means the source says so but the paper doesn't confirm it — like English "the accident reportedly happened…". You need to recognise it; you don't need to use it when speaking.
o português também tem esses recursos: «: English "He denied that it was true" keeps the indicative; Spanish switches: «Negó que fuera cierto». English "reportedly / allegedly" often corresponds to the rumour conditional: «habría ocurrido». And after «afirmar», «asegurar» and «anunciar» there's no «de»: «afirmó que», never «afirmó de que».

Falar de notícias, redes sociais e verif: Talking about news, social media and fact-checking
PASSO 1: para puxar assunto: «¿Has visto: STEP 1: to bring up a topic: «¿Has visto la noticia de…?» (Have you seen the story about…?), «He leído que…», «Me suena que…» (I seem to remember that…). STEP 2: to express doubt: «No me fío de esa página.» (I don't trust that website.), «Desconfío de ese titular.», «No sé si es verdad.» «Fiarse de» and «confiar en» mean the same but take different prepositions. STEP 3: to give advice, use the negative imperative, which uses the subjunctive (lesson 28): «No compartas una noticia sin comprobar la fuente.» and the affirmative: «Comprueba la fuente.» STEP 4: to generalise: «Hay que comprobar la fuente» (You have to check the source), «Conviene leer más de un periódico.» STEP 5: use impersonal «se» for collective habits: «Se comparte mucha información falsa por las redes.» (A lot of false information is shared on social media.)
em português «confiar em» e «desconfiar: English "to trust" has no preposition, and "trust IN" exists too. Spanish fixes it: «confiar EN» and «fiarse DE»: «Confío en él», «Me fío de él». So "I don't trust that site" = «No me fío de esa página». And "to check" in this sense is «comprobar», not «chequear» (used colloquially in Latin America, but avoid it in careful Spanish).
